unit.prompt_vi: Người phụ nữ gánh hàng rong trên phố vào buổi sáng.
unit.P_orig: A woman carrying a shoulder pole of street goods along a street in the morning.
unit.P_ct: A woman carrying a shoulder pole of street goods along a street in the morning. In the early morning of a bustling Vietnamese market street, a woman carries a traditional Vietnamese street vending cart known as a "gánh hàng rong" (a balanced pole across her shoulders with robust, intricately woven bamboo baskets on either end) — a practice that has been a cornerstone of Vietnamese markets for centuries, reflecting the country’s cultural resilience and entrepreneurial spirit. The pole and baskets are made of lightweight and durable bamboo, a traditional material in Vietnam that ensures the cart is both strong and easy to handle. The baskets, resembling large woven shopping bags but more robust and intricately designed, are filled with fresh fruits and vegetables in vibrant colors and textures, such as ripe oranges, crisp lettuce, and fresh tomatoes. The woman carefully navigates the narrow pathway, maintaining her balance as she sets off to sell her wares for the day. The market is already alive with activity, vendors shouting prices and the clinking of metal containers, customers bargaining over the day’s fresh catch, creating a vibrant tapestry of sights, sounds, and scents like the aroma of freshly brewed coffee and the sight of colorful flowers. The "gánh hàng rong" not only serves as a means of livelihood for many Vietnamese but also preserves a rich cultural tradition that dates back generations, embodying the spirit of ingenuity and resilience that defines Vietnamese culture.

=== PASSAGE [vi] Gánh hàng rong — https://vi.wikipedia.org/wiki/G%C3%A1nh_h%C3%A0ng_rong ===
Gánh hàng rong hay còn gọi là lái buôn, con buôn, người đi chào hàng là một người bán hàng gánh lưu động và không cố định một chỗ. Ở Anh, từ "peddler" dùng để chỉ những người lang thang đi bán rong từ nông thôn cho đến các thị trấn, làng quê nhỏ bé. Tại Luân Đôn, người ta dùng những từ chỉ cụ thể hơn là "costermonger" để chỉ người bán hàng rau quả. Từ nguyên và định nghĩa trong tiếng Anh Gánh hàng rong, theo luật pháp của nước Anh, được định nghĩa là: "bất kỳ một người bán hàng rong, gánh hàng rong, tiểu thương, thợ hàn nồi, thợ đúc kim loại, thợ sửa ghế hay một người nào đó mà không có ngựa hay súc vật khác đi cùng hoặc kéo chở, đi bộ từ nơi này qua nơi khác để giao dịch buôn bán và đi từ thị trấn này tới thị trấn kia hoặc tới nhà người khác, mang theo để rao hàng hay bày bán bất kỳ đồ vật, sản phẩm hàng hóa nào một cách trực tiếp để được giao hàng và chở tới nơi, hoặc rao bán hay mời bán tay nghề thủ công." === PASSAGE [en] Carrying pole — https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carrying_pole ===
A carrying pole, also called a shoulder pole or a milkmaid's yoke, is a yoke of wood or bamboo, used by people to carry a load. This piece of equipment is used in one of two basic ways: A single person balances the yoke over one shoulder, with an evenly distributed load being suspended from each end. Two people support the yoke by resting it on a shoulder, with the load suspended from the centre of the yoke. The individual carries the device by balancing the yoke upon one or both shoulders. The Western milkmaid's yoke is fitted over both shoulders. However, the East Asian type is carried on one shoulder. In ancient Greece, it was called asilla (ἄσιλλα) or anaphoron (ἀνάφορον) and was a wooden pole or yoke carried by a person, either across both shoulders or, more commonly, on one shoulder and used for transporting burdens. Types Canoe Many canoes include a thwart shaped like a yoke to aid in carrying the boat. The bamboo yoke is normally between 1 and 1.5 meters in length, and carried with the curved (outside surface) of the bamboo against the shoulder. The carrying pole has distinct advantages over the vending cart, the other main manual conveyance of goods in East Asia. The carrying pole can be transported within a motorized vehicle. Independent vendors are also often allowed to transport their carrying poles on intercity buses, and can be seen entering cities to sell their goods.
